questions.explanation: `a` is a 2D array. In memory, it is stored row by row as a contiguous block: `1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9`. `int *ptr = (int *)a;` makes `ptr` point to the very first element of the 2D array, which is `a[0][0]` (value 1). `*(ptr + 4)`: `ptr + 4` moves the pointer 4 integer positions forward from `a[0][0]`. This points to `a[1][1]` (value 5). Dereferencing it gives 5. `*(*(a + 1) + 2)`: `a` is a pointer to an array of 3 integers (`int (*)[3]`). `a + 1` moves `a` one full row forward (3 integers * `sizeof(int)`). So `(a + 1)` points to the second row, which is `&a[1]`. `*(a + 1)` dereferences this, giving the second row itself (which is equivalent to `a[1]`). When used in an expression, `a[1]` decays to a pointer to its first element, `&a[1][0]`. `(*(a + 1) + 2)` moves this pointer two integer positions forward from `a[1][0]`. This points to `a[1][2]`. `*(*(a + 1) + 2)` dereferences it, giving the value `a[1][2]`, which is 6. The output will be `5 6`.
